questions.stem: A cell appears 30 mm wide in a microscope image taken at x500 magnification. What is the actual size of the cell?
questions.explanation: Using the formula: actual size = image size / magnification = 30 mm / 500 = 0.06 mm = 60 micrometres. This is a typical size for an animal cell. A common error is to multiply instead of divide.

questions.stem: A student measures a cell as 50 micrometres across. How would this be expressed in standard form?
questions.explanation: One micrometre = 1 x 10^-6 m. So 50 micrometres = 50 x 10^-6 m = 5 x 10^-5 m in standard form. Standard form requires a number between 1 and 10 multiplied by a power of 10.

questions.stem: A drawing of a cell is 60 mm long. The actual cell is 0.12 mm long. What is the magnification of the drawing?
questions.explanation: Magnification = image size / actual size = 60 mm / 0.12 mm = x500. The units must be the same for both measurements before dividing. The magnification has no units.

questions.stem: A scale bar on a micrograph is labelled '10 micrometres' and measures 20 mm on the image. A structure in the same image measures 5 mm. What is the actual size of the structure?
questions.explanation: First find the magnification from the scale bar: magnification = 20 mm / 0.01 mm (10 micrometres) = x2000. Then: actual size = image size / magnification = 5 mm / 2000 = 0.0025 mm = 2.5 micrometres.

questions.stem: A bacterium is 2 micrometres long and a human cheek cell is 60 micrometres long. How many times larger is the cheek cell than the bacterium?
questions.explanation: To compare sizes: 60 micrometres / 2 micrometres = 30 times. The cheek cell is 30 times larger than the bacterium. This illustrates the significant size difference between prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells.
